title: Clinical and Radiological Significance of Anatomical Variations in Paranasal Sinuses: A Retrospective CT-Based Study
summary: A retrospective CT-based study explored the clinical and radiological importance of anatomical variations in the paranasal sinuses. The work emphasizes how variants such as septal deviation, concha bullosa, Haller and Onodi cells, and frontal recess anatomy can influence disease presentation, surgical planning, and complication risk. Accurate CT reporting and preoperative recognition of these variants are critical to improving outcomes and minimizing intraoperative injury.
content:
Background and purpose:
Anatomical variations of the paranasal sinuses are common and often incidental on imaging, yet they can have important clinical and surgical consequences. Retrospective CT analyses provide a reliable method to catalog variants and to evaluate their potential association with sinonasal disease, obstructive symptoms, and risks during endoscopic sinus surgery. This article summarizes the clinical and radiological significance of those variations and outlines practical implications for reporting and surgical planning.

Common anatomical variations:
Common variants encountered on coronal and axial CT include nasal septal deviation, concha bullosa (pneumatization of the middle turbinate), agger nasi cells, Haller (infraorbital) cells, Onodi cells (sphenoethmoidal air cells), frontal recess variants, and variations in the size and pneumatization of the sphenoid sinus. Each of these can alter normal drainage pathways, narrow ostiomeatal complexes, or place critical structures such as the orbit, optic nerve, and internal carotid artery in closer proximity to surgical corridors.

Clinical relevance:
While many variations are asymptomatic, certain configurations predispose to recurrent or chronic sinusitis by impairing ventilation and mucociliary clearance. For example, a concha bullosa or significant septal deviation may contribute to obstructed drainage in the middle meatus. Haller cells and frontal recess anatomy can complicate drainage of the maxillary and frontal sinuses respectively. Recognizing these patterns helps clinicians correlate imaging with symptoms and guides conservative versus surgical management decisions.

Radiological assessment and reporting:
High-resolution CT with coronal and axial reconstructions remains the imaging standard for preoperative assessment. Radiology reports should systematically document variant anatomy and any anatomical relationships to the orbit, optic nerve, and carotid canal. A focused checklist style report aids otolaryngologists in planning, highlighting variants that increase operative difficulty or risk.

Implications for endoscopic sinus surgery:
Unrecognized variants increase the risk of intraoperative complications such as orbital injury, cerebrospinal fluid leak, or damage to the optic nerve or carotid artery. Preoperative awareness allows surgeons to adapt approaches, anticipate altered landmarks, and counsel patients appropriately. In addition, tailored surgical strategies (for example limited turbinate reduction or targeted ethmoidectomy) can address obstructive variants while minimizing morbidity.

Limitations of retrospective CT studies:
Retrospective analyses are valuable for mapping variant prevalence and potential associations with disease, but they have limitations. Correlation with clinical symptoms, endoscopic findings, and surgical outcomes is necessary to determine the true clinical impact of any variant. Interobserver variability in identifying and classifying cells and pneumatization patterns can also affect reproducibility.

Recommendations and conclusion:
Clinicians and radiologists should adopt a consistent approach to describing paranasal sinus anatomy on CT. Structured reporting that flags variants with potential surgical or clinical relevance improves multidisciplinary communication. Further prospective and outcome-linked studies would clarify which variants most strongly predict disease or complications, helping refine indications for intervention. For now, careful preoperative imaging review remains a cornerstone of safe and effective management of sinonasal disease.
